MUQATIL:18:13-17/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r2.claim: God strengthened their hearts with faith; they stood on their feet and declared God alone Lord of heaven and earth.

MUQATIL:18:13-17/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r3.claim: They will not worship a deity besides God; doing so would be a grave injustice against Him.

MUQATIL:18:13-17/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:13-17/r4.claim: Shataṭ means injustice; he links it with 38:22 and 72:4.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r1.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r1.claim: Qatāda says God strengthened the youths' hearts with faith.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r2.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p174/r2.claim: Qatāda explains their denouncing a rival deity as calling it a gross falsehood.

MAJAZ:v1p394/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p394/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p394/r2.claim: The anonymous verse uses ashaṭṭa for going too far or acting unjustly.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r1.claim: God strengthened their hearts by inspiring patience and making them steadfast.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p264#2/r2.claim: Shaṭaṭ means excess or extremity; ashṭa ʿalayya means he went too far in speech.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r3.claim: The youths followed Jesus, while their idolatrous king pressed them to worship idols; they refused and withdrew to a cave to protect their faith.

TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.speaker: عمرو
TAB-FULL:v15p161/r4.claim: One youth proposed his father's cave as refuge; the people sealed them inside, then a later Christian king removed the barrier, whereupon they awoke and estimated they had slept a day or part of one.

TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r1.claim: As Deqianus prepared a citywide sacrifice to idols, the youths prayed for the believers' deliverance; informers found them prostrate and reported their disobedience to the king.

TAB-FULL:v15p166/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r3.speaker: مكسلمينا
TAB-FULL:v15p166/r3.claim: Their spokesman declares that the Lord of heaven and earth alone is their God; they will worship and ask help only of Him, never idols or devils.

TAB-FULL:v15p173/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p173/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v15p173/r2.claim: Mujahid says the youths were noble sons who gathered unexpectedly; their eldest voiced belief in the Lord of heaven and earth, the others agreed, and all decided to enter the cave.

TAB-FULL:v15p178/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p178/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p178/r3.claim: God inspired patience and strengthened their hearts with the light of faith, so that they could give up their former comfort.

TAB-FULL:v15p178/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p178/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v15p178/r4.claim: Qatada explains that their hearts were strengthened through faith.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r1.claim: The youths spoke to Deqianus when he reproached them for refusing his gods; their Lord owns the heavens and earth, whereas his idols are created beings, so they would not worship them.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r2.claim: Calling on any god besides the Lord of heaven and earth would be an outrageous, exaggerated falsehood that exceeds the bounds of truth.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r3.claim: In the idiom for bidding, shatata means to exceed the proper measure; distance and height have different forms of the root.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r4.speaker: الشاعر
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r4.claim: The cited poet's phrase ashatat witnesses the sense of exceeding the proper limit.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r5.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r5.claim: Qatada glosses shatata as a lie.

TAB-FULL:v15p179/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v15p179/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses shatata as erroneous speech.

ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r2.claim: The youths say they would have spoken an unjust falsehood by invoking another deity; شططا is a cognate accusative from شط and أشط, to act unjustly.

ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p271#2/r3.claim: An unattributed poem uses أشطت of unjust excess and witnesses this verb's meaning.

NAHHAS:v2p450/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p450/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p450/r2.claim: God strengthened the youths’ hearts so they could speak firmly in front of unbelievers; shaṭaṭan is a verbal noun meaning extreme speech and may also be an object of ‘said.’

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r1.claim: God marked their secrets with the Real and made them stand through and for Him; calling Him our Lord expresses desire and invocation, while Lord of heaven and earth abandons personal attributes for His; invoking no other deity means relying on no one else.

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r2.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r2.claim: God strengthened their hearts so they fulfilled the covenant and cleared their secrets of everything besides Him.

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r3.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r3.claim: Their rising means that they stood and prayed to God sincerely.

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r4.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r4.claim: They rose away from distraction with created things, looking to and resting in nothing besides God.

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r5.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r5.claim: They stood before God with decorum, truthful invocation, neediness, and refuge; God answered with subtle words and wondrous signs.

SULAMI:v1p404#2/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r6.speaker: بعض مشايخنا
SULAMI:v1p404#2/r6.claim: The verse supports movement among ecstatic worshippers during audition and remembrance: hearts tied to the unseen realm are moved by lights of remembrance and audition.

THALABI:v6p147#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147#2/r1.claim: The guards find the youths prostrating in their prayer place, weeping and asking God to save them from Daqyanus and his faction.

THALABI:v6p147#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147#2/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147#2/r2.claim: Daqyanus demands that the youths sacrifice to the idols or face execution.

THALABI:v6p147#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147#2/r3.speaker: مكسلمينا
THALABI:v6p147#2/r3.claim: Their eldest, Maksalmina, declares that they worship only the Lord of heaven and earth and will never accept the tyrant's idols.

THALABI:v6p147#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147#2/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147#2/r4.claim: The companions of Maksalmina answer Daqyanus with the same confession of faith.

THALABI:v6p147#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147#2/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147#2/r5.claim: The ruler postpones punishment because they are young, strips their rank clothing and gold and silver adornments, and gives them time to reconsider.

THALABI:v6p147/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق
THALABI:v6p147/r1.claim: Ibn Ishaq narrates that pagan Roman ruler Decius persecuted Christians in Ephesus; eight noble youths kept monotheism, prayed and fasted, then fled the forced choice between idol worship and death after believers were tortured and displayed on the city walls.

THALABI:v6p147/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p147/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p147/r2.claim: The youths' prayer declares God alone as Lord of heaven and earth and says invoking another deity would be an outrageous falsehood; they ask for the persecution to be lifted.

THALABI:v6p149/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p149/r5.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
THALABI:v6p149/r5.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr describes noble, adorned youths who secretly came to faith during a festival where their people displayed idols.

THALABI:v6p149/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p149/r6.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
THALABI:v6p149/r6.claim: In Ubayd ibn Umayr's account, the youths separately confide their faith to one another and discover that they share one belief.

THALABI:v6p150/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p150/r3.speaker: وهب بن منبه
THALABI:v6p150/r3.claim: Wahb says a disciple of Jesus avoids a city's idol, works at a bathhouse, and teaches young men about heaven, earth, and the afterlife until they believe.

THALABI:v6p150/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p150/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه
THALABI:v6p150/r4.claim: In Wahb's account, the disciple rebukes the prince's son for entering a bath with a woman; both die there, and the disciple is blamed and pursued.

THALABI:v6p158/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p158/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p158/r10.claim: God strengthens their hearts with patience and the light of faith so they can leave comfortable homes and their people for the cave.

THALABI:v6p158/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p158/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p158/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas and Muqatil gloss shatat as injustice or wrong.

THALABI:v6p158/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p158/r12.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v6p158/r12.claim: Qatada glosses shatat as a lie.

THALABI:v6p158/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p158/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p158/r13.claim: The root of shatat means going beyond the proper measure and excess.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r12.claim: Another account says they were noble young men who met outside the city by chance; their eldest professed the Lord of heaven and earth, they agreed, then entered the cave and remained for three hundred years plus nine.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r14.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r14.claim: شططا means a lie or falsehood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r15.speaker: الأخفش
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p286#2/r15.claim: شططا may mean excess or extremism.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r1.claim: ربطنا على قلوبهم means that God strengthened their hearts.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r2.speaker: اليزيدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r2.claim: Alternatively, God inspired their hearts to be patient.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r3.claim: شططا may mean excess or extremism.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p289/r4.claim: شططا may also mean remoteness or going far astray.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r10.claim: One reading says God bound their hearts by effacing awareness of everything besides Him and freeing them from reflection through insight.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r11.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r11.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r11.claim: Another reading says their hearts were filled with proofs from the unseen, leaving no room for conjecture or satanic whispers.

QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p209/r9.claim: God strengthened their hearts with increased certainty, removing doubt and completing their tranquility.

QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r1.claim: The youths stood for God through God; one who stands by God turns from everything else, and one who stands for God continues until reaching Him.

QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r2.claim: Attributing events to created contingencies as independent causes is shirk; claiming events come from other than God makes that other thing a deity.

QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p211/r3.claim: A religious claim without rational or transmitted proof is fabrication; a spiritual state must be earned through sincere striving, and the truthful hear inwardly from the Real before speaking.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r2.claim: God strengthened their hearts with patience and certainty as they stood before a king who forced people away from their religions.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:13-16/r3.claim: They proclaimed the Lord of the heavens and earth alone, saying that worship of another god would be a gross falsehood.

JISHUMI:v6p4363/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4363/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4363/r4.claim: Rabṭ means binding or tightening; a person with a firm heart is described as rābiṭ al-jāsh.

JISHUMI:v6p4363/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4363/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4363/r8.claim: Shaṭaṭ is exceeding a boundary through remoteness or extravagance, and by extension means going far beyond the proper limit.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r2.claim: God strengthened their hearts with patience and faith, helping them leave their prosperous, honored life and flee to the cave for their religion.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r3.claim: They stood before Daqyānūs after he reproached them for abandoning idol worship and declared God alone Lord of heaven and earth.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r4.claim: He glosses shaṭaṭan as injustice; its root conveys going beyond the limit.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r5.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p156/r5.claim: He glosses shaṭaṭan as a lie.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r2.claim: God strengthened their hearts to endure leaving home and comfort, flee with their faith, and publicly speak the truth.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r3.claim: They stood before the tyrant Diqyānūs without fear when he reproached them for abandoning idol worship.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p661/r4.claim: Shataṭan is an excessively wrongful and extreme statement, from a root meaning to go far away.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r4.claim: Tying their hearts is a metaphor for the resolve and patience God gave them; firmness is pictured as binding what fear might loosen.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r5.claim: Their standing and speaking may describe their courageous appearance before the unbelieving king, when they rejected his religion despite threats.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r6.claim: Alternatively, standing means resolving firmly to flee to God and oppose their people; this better fits the following advice about leaving them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r7.speaker: الأعمش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r7.claim: Al-A'mash reads 'when they stood, standing, and said,' adding qiyāman.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p500#3/r8.claim: Shatatan means injustice, crossing a limit, or excess; the related verb describes overpricing and the root also conveys distance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p501/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p501/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p501/r11.claim: The following verse, attributed in the preceding passage to an unnamed poet, illustrates shatata as going too far in reproach.

TABRISI:18:13-14/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:13-14/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:13-14/r10.claim: God strengthened their hearts with faith-firming graces and thoughts so they could proclaim truth, endure hardship, and leave home.

TABRISI:18:13-14/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:13-14/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:13-14/r11.claim: They spoke before Daqiyānūs, the tyrant who tested believers, declaring that their Lord created the heavens and earth and that calling on another god would be an extreme falsehood.

TABRISI:18:13-14/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:18:13-14/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:18:13-14/r4.claim: Shataṭ means exceeding a boundary through excess; the root evokes remoteness, and the same root can describe excessive height or overpricing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r1.claim: Increasing their guidance means making them firm in faith; strengthening their hearts means inspiring patience.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r2.claim: They stood before their king Decianus, who called people to worship idols; God protected them so they could defy him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r3.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r3.claim: They stood among their people and called them to affirm God's oneness.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r4.claim: Another view is that they spoke these words among themselves after gathering outside the city, as recounted earlier.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r5.claim: شطط means injustice or excessive wrong.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p115#2/r6.claim: The verbs شط and أشط mean to act unjustly.

RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r3.claim: Mujāhid says they were city notables who gathered outside without arranging it, and one disclosed that he felt their Lord was Lord of the heavens and earth.

RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r4.claim: A second account says they stood before the tyrant Daqyānūs, confessed God as Lord of the heavens and earth, and were divinely strengthened to resist him and renounce partners.

RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r5.speaker: عطاء ومقاتل
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r5.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Muqātil say they made the declaration on waking, but Rāzī finds this unlikely because the account is introduced afterward as a new narration.

RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r6.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r6.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains shataṭ as going beyond the limit; its root imagery is distance, so it means straying far from truth, and it functions as a cognate accusative.

RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
RAZI-FULL:v21p83#2/r7.claim: Al-Zajjāj and others also recognize shatta or ashatta for exceeding the limit.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14#2/r1.speaker: أبو بكر الطرسوسي
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14#2/r1.claim: Asked about Sufi practice, al-Tarsusi says dancing and ecstatic display began with the Samiri's people, who danced around the calf; he calls it pagan worship.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r1.claim: Tying their hearts means God gave them firm resolve and patience to confess God's sole lordship before unbelievers; fear resembles loosening, while courage resembles binding.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r2.claim: The image also appears in the account of Moses' mother and in 8:11, where God binds hearts and steadies feet.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r3.claim: The youths' standing may describe their confrontation before the pagan king, where rejecting his religion required strength against his power.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r4.claim: Another account says noble youths gathered outside town without appointment; their eldest voiced a conviction about God and the others affirmed it together.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r5.claim: A third interpretation takes standing as their decisive resolve to flee to God and oppose their people.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r6.claim: Shatatan means a grossly unjust or impossible statement: invoking another deity would be a wrong and falsehood.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r7.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r7.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Sufis rely on the youths' standing and speaking as a basis for devotional practice.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r8.claim: Al-Qurtubi rejects that inference: the youths praised God, thanked Him, then fled in fear, which has no relation to foot-stamping or dancing to attractive voices.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:14/r9.claim: He says such dancing is forbidden according to a group of scholars and points to his discussion of 17:37.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r1.claim: God strengthened the youths' hearts to endure abandoning home, family, and property and to confront the tyrant Daqyanus with the truth.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:14-18/r2.claim: They stood before the ruler and declared that God alone rules the heavens and earth; invoking another deity would be an extreme departure from truth.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r1.claim: God strengthened their hearts to endure abandoning their homes and fleeing for faith, and emboldened them to proclaim the truth and profess Islam.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r2.claim: They stood before the tyrant Diqyanus without fear when he reproached them for abandoning idol worship.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r3.claim: They proudly declare God alone is Lord of the heavens and earth; calling another god would be excessive injustice and falsehood.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p5#4/r4.claim: Shaṭaṭ means excessive injustice and going too far, from a root meaning to be distant.

QASHANI:18:13-15/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:13-15/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:13-15/r2.claim: God strengthened them for struggle against Satan and ego, abandoning bodily familiarity and desire and proclaiming unity against the soul's worship of body and caprice despite threats of poverty and death.

QASHANI:18:13-15/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:18:13-15/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:18:13-15/r3.claim: Alternatively, God emboldened them to proclaim true religion against tyrants such as Daqyanus, Nimrod, Pharaoh, and Abu Jahl, who claim lordship through rebellious ego.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p132/r7.claim: Shaṭaṭ means injustice, exceeding a limit, and going to extremes; al-Farrāʾ also gives related lexical forms for excess, distance, wronging, and height.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r10.claim: ربطنا على قلوبهم means God steadied and strengthened them to endure exile, abandon comfort, and flee with their faith to a desolate cave.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r11.claim: The binding metaphor fits because fear seems to unravel the self, while a firm heart resembles something tied fast; رابط الجأش is the related idiom.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p148/r12.claim: The verb governing إذ is ربطنا, so the strengthening happened when they stood; the passage begins to offer possible senses of their standing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r1.claim: قاموا may mean they resolved with utmost seriousness to flee to God and separate from their people.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r10.claim: If spoken before the king, their rebuke publicly repudiates his idolatry and undermines his authority; if spoken while departing, it marks their resolve.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r11.speaker: الحوفي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r11.claim: Al-Ḥawfī parses قومنا as the predicate of هؤلاء and اتخذوا as a circumstantial clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r12.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r12.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū al-Baqāʾ parse قومنا as an apposition and اتخذوا as the predicate.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r13.claim: لولا is an exhortation shaped by rebuke, not a straightforward demand for proof, since a manifest proof for idolatry is impossible; it challenges them to expose their inability.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r14.claim: اتخذوا can mean they fashioned the idols themselves, or that they made them into gods.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r15.claim: The passage establishes that religious belief requires proof; an unsupported claim is false and an unjust fabrication of partners for God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r2.speaker: الكرماني
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r2.claim: Al-Kirmānī says قاموا means that the youths stood on their feet.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r3.claim: Another view is that the youths secretly called their people to God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r4.speaker: عطاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r4.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says they stood when waking from sleep; another reported view says they stood firm in faith.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r5.speaker: صاحب الغنيان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r5.claim: The author of al-Ghunyān says they stood before the king; a cat or mouse startled him, and the youths then declared God alone Lord of heaven and earth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r6.claim: Their confession identifies God as creator and sovereign over the heavens and earth, then emphatically disavows every other deity; شطط means transgression and injustice.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r7.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r7.claim: Qatāda glosses شططا as a lie.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r8.speaker: أبو زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r8.claim: Abū Zayd glosses شططا as an error.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p149/r9.claim: The youths condemn their people’s baseless worship and the enormity of fabricating partners for God; their speech may be before the king or as they set out to flee.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r1.claim: إذ قاموا is governed by ربطنا; الربط metaphorically strengthens their hearts in a perilous place.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r2.claim: إذًا is a جواب and result: if they worshipped another god, they would have uttered outrageous words.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r3.claim: شطط derives from going beyond a limit; related uses include overpricing, distance, and height.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r4.claim: Sibawayh parses شططا as circumstantial to the understood verbal noun of قلنا.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r5.claim: Alternatively, it modifies an omitted قول or emphatically restates the verbal noun.

SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:14/r6.claim: A third analysis makes شططا an object of قلنا because it contains the meaning of a sentence.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r1.claim: God strengthened their hearts to endure opposing their people and leaving prosperous lives; reports describe them as sons of Roman kings and nobles under the tyrant Daqyanus, who demanded idol worship and sacrifice.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r2.claim: Seeing their people bow to and sacrifice for idols, the youths recognized that worship belongs only to the Creator of the heavens and earth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r3.claim: Aisha's report, also transmitted by Muslim from Abu Hurayra, says souls are gathered troops: those that recognize each other unite and those that do not differ.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r4.claim: The youths disclosed their belief one by one and found that all shared it; they united in worship, were discovered and denounced, then told the king the truth and called him to God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p140#2/r5.claim: The wording 'we will never invoke' expresses permanent negation; invoking another god would be a falsehood, lie, and slander.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r4.claim: God strengthened their hearts by gathering their inner powers rather than letting them disperse, making them steadfast in public as in private.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r5.claim: They stood before the unbelieving generation's tyrant, Decius, and declared that the Lord of heaven and earth alone deserves worship.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p449/r6.claim: They reject invoking any deity besides God as an extreme departure from truth, since all others are incapable and lack evidence.

DURR-FULL:v5p365/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r2.claim: The youths lived under an idolatrous tyrant who forced the people to worship idols; they left the city and God gathered them unexpectedly in the wilderness.

DURR-FULL:v5p365/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p365/r3.claim: At first the youths concealed their reasons for leaving, then made mutual pledges to disclose their aims and united in affirming that the Lord of the heavens and earth alone is God.

DURR-FULL:v5p370/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p370/r11.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v5p370/r11.claim: Ibn Zayd explains شطط as mistaken speech.

DURR-FULL:v5p370/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p370/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p370/r8.claim: God strengthened the youths' hearts through faith.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r1.claim: God strengthened the youths to bear leaving home and comfort and to proclaim truth before the tyrant; speaking truth to a ruler is the best jihad because the ruler exposes its speaker to mortal danger.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r2.claim: Rabt literally ties an animal with a tether; figuratively, God tying a heart means giving it patience and firmness against fear.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r3.claim: The syntax attaches إذ قاموا to ربطنا, and their standing means rising to display the religious creed.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r4.speaker: قيل
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r4.claim: An alternative takes their standing as standing fearlessly before Decianus; on this reading their later words beginning هؤلاء follow their departure from him.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r5.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r5.claim: The inward binding keeps the youths from worldly adornments and turns them wholly toward God; after awakening they preferred divine nearness to worldly life.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r6.claim: God is creator and owner of the world; an idol is a created part of it and cannot be worshipped. The youths will never worship another deity, directly or in partnership.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r7.claim: Calling idols gods rather than lords explains why the text says إله and directly rebuts the opponents' terminology.

BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p171#2/r8.claim: Shطط means speech exceeding the proper limit, either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun or as an intensive verbal noun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r1.claim: God steadied their hearts with patience so separation from home, family, comfort, friends, the tyrant, and the crowd of unbelievers would not shake them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r10.claim: God's lordship over heaven and earth entails lordship over everything in them, including the youths, so they begin with that premise and then reject every other deity.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r11.claim: They use lan because it is more emphatic than other negators and may cover all time: they will never worship another deity, alone or alongside God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r12.claim: They say ilah rather than rabb to reject their opponents' naming idols as gods and to identify divinity as the basis of worship; the phrases can also express distinct lordship and worship monotheisms.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r13.claim: Idolaters acknowledge God's lordship as creator but deny exclusive worship, claiming idols bring them nearer to God and reciting a formula that gives Him a partner He owns.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r14.claim: The youths state lordship first as the first rank of monotheism and a gradual challenge: exclusive lordship entails exclusive divinity, which God argues against polytheists elsewhere.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r15.claim: Another reading takes the first clause itself to indicate exclusive worship, making the second clause reinforce it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r2.claim: “Binding” the heart is metaphorical; lexicons use binding for fastening an animal and figuratively for giving someone patience and steadfast resolve.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r3.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r3.claim: Al-Kashf explains the metaphor by contrasting panic that makes hearts rise to the throats with a heart made firm and settled.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r4.claim: Some analyze the phrase as an implicit metaphor made vivid, with ʿala used despite the verb's usual direct-object construction.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r5.claim: Their “standing” means resolutely setting out toward God and opposing their people, like the idiom “so-and-so undertook” an action; it may also mean standing to proclaim religion.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r6.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says they left the city, met by chance, and one voiced his conviction that his Lord was Lord of heaven and earth, which the others shared.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas's account has them first concealing their intentions, then making a pledge before agreeing on their shared confession.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r8.speaker: صاحب الغنيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r8.claim: The Ghunyān says they stood before King Daqyanus; a cat or mouse frightened him, and the youths blurted out their confession without fear.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r9.speaker: عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p218#2/r9.claim: Ata says their standing was rising from sleep, but the author dismisses this and the similar claim that it means remaining firm in faith.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r1.claim: The phrase “from apart from Him” modifies the following indefinite noun in a circumstantial construction, or qualifies it if placed after the noun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r2.claim: Shatatan means a statement far from truth, either a verbal noun or a source used adjectivally for emphatic effect.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r3.claim: Abu al-Baqa permits shatatan as the direct object of “we said.”

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r4.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r4.claim: Qatada glosses shatatan as a lie; Ibn Zayd says error and al-Suddi says injustice, all derivative senses of excessive distance from truth.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r5.claim: The root shatta denotes moving too far away, as illustrated by a cited line of poetry.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r6.claim: An omitted oath is answered by the emphatic lam; idha is conditional or responsive, with the implied condition that invoking another god would be an outrageous statement.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p219/r7.claim: Worship necessarily entails acknowledging and petitioning a deity, so the speech implies that the youths were urged to worship idols and reproached for refusing, consistent with their standing before the king.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r11.claim: God steadied their hearts with certainty, removing intrusive guesses and Satanic whispers; another reading says He raised them from spiritual fluctuation to firmness.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r12.claim: Their standing is allegorized as standing through God; He alone sustains and governs the heavens and earth, which exist through His generosity.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r13.speaker: بعض المشايخ
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r13.claim: Some shaykhs cite the youths' standing as proof that spiritual seekers should stand while remembering God; Ibn al-Ghars calls the proof weak. Al-Ālūsī allows standing remembrance but condemns the contemporary ritual circles as lacking prophetic precedent and as snares of Satan.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r10.claim: They entrusted Yemliha with provisions; he entered town disguised as a poor man, bought what was needed, and returned with news.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r11.claim: After the emperor returned, the youths prayed and fell asleep; God moved him to wall up the cave as their tomb.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r12.claim: Two believers in the emperor's household, Pendros and Runas, concealed the youths' names, lineage, and story on lead tablets in a copper case inside the wall.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r15.claim: They call any deity besides God impossible and false, so claiming another god is irrational and a lie.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r4.claim: God strengthened their hearts, giving them firmness and resolve.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r5.claim: Their defining act was to rise against polytheists and publicly proclaim God's oneness.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r8.claim: When the emperor offered worship of idols or death, the youths rejected the invitation and professed faith in their one Lord.

ELMALILI:18:13-14/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:13-14/r9.claim: After being dismissed with time to reconsider, they resolved to protect their faith by fleeing to a steep cave on Mount Benclus near the city.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r1.claim: The youths most likely addressed their polytheist people publicly to declare faith and defy the king’s threat; Ibn Ashur compares their stance with Israel before Pharaoh.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r2.claim: An alternative is that they spoke privately while indirectly admonishing their people, using an allusive address to draw them toward the truth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r3.claim: If the statement was private among the youths, ‘Lord of the heavens and earth’ is an explanatory apposition and the following clause is the predicate; if public, it informs their people and the next clause resumes the speech.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r4.claim: They mention supplication rather than worship because supplication covers every verbal act, including ascribing divinity to others and calling on them for needs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p273/r5.claim: The oath-marked statement about speaking wildly explains the emphatic negation; shataṭ means excessive departure from truth, figuratively derived from distance from home.

TABATABAI:18:26#4/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:26#4/r6.claim: The youths’ departure was migration from a society that prevented open monotheism and threatened stoning or forced conversion; their declaration at some point does not rule out taqiyya earlier.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r1.claim: Their coordinated flight and abandonment of family, property, and homeland showed opposition, but their first declaration can be understood as private resolve rather than public defiance; either way, the verses allow taqiyya earlier.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#29/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the youths left separately from an idolatrous city and cautiously questioned one another before making pledges, agreeing that God alone is Lord and seeking refuge in the cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r6.claim: Al-Baqir glosses shatatan as injustice against God if one claims He has a partner.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.claim: The Qurʾānic narrative first shows the youths’ truth-bearing withdrawal and long sleep, then their awakening and exchange that exposes them, and finally their discovery and the mosque built over them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r2.claim: The youths lived amid idol worship and were persecuted for their informed monotheistic faith; God increased their guidance, knowledge, and wisdom and strengthened their hearts against fear.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r3.claim: Seeing that remaining would force them to conceal truth or conform to idolatry, the youths chose to affirm God as Lord of heaven and earth, reject other gods as false, and withdraw to the cave trusting in divine mercy and guidance.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r1.claim: Rabt means binding; strengthening hearts is a metaphor for removing their anxiety and agitation. Shataṭ is exceeding truth, and sulṭān is proof.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r2.claim: The verses recount the youths' first public argument against paganism, targeting the supposed divinity of angels, jinn, and revered humans rather than the idols that merely depict them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#6/r3.claim: The rational pronoun in the command to bring proof against the claimed gods supports the reading that the argument targets rational beings.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r1.claim: They affirm one Lord of heaven and earth against paganism's separate deity for each created kind, then deny all other gods, including the higher beings claimed by some traditions.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r2.claim: Calling any creature divine exceeds proper bounds by elevating it to the Creator's rank.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r3.claim: Their demand for clear proof answers the polytheists' appeal that God is too exalted to perceive directly: all creatures know God through His names, attributes, and effects according to capacity.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r4.claim: Creation, provision, ownership, and governance belong to God alone, so only He possesses the attributes that merit worship.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#7/r6.claim: The wording implies they spoke openly amid coercive idol worship, not in private; denying gods after affirming God's lordship hints that they were compelled to invoke idols.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r1.claim: They most likely rose during an assembly enforcing idol worship, publicly declared monotheism, and fled under mortal threat; a report that six were the king's advisers supports this.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r2.claim: Public confession does not conflict with reports that they had concealed their faith: they could have practiced caution before suddenly declaring belief and leaving.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#8/r3.claim: Other readings take their standing as rising for God, or place the speeches after they left town; on these readings their strengthened hearts meant they feared no consequence of flight.

ASAD-NOTES:18:13#n15/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:13#n15/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:13#n15/r1.claim: Their standing up means confronting misguided fellow people or persecuting rulers.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: God's strengthening of their hearts enabled the young believers to proclaim monotheism despite the difficulty of calling their people to truth.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The word shatat means drawing away from truth; the youths refused to retreat privately after believing and instead undertook public preaching.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:13/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:13/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:13/r1.claim: Unable to profess or practice monotheism safely amid persecution, the youths left their people with their dog and sought refuge in the cave.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r1.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r1.claim: The Quran stresses the Companions’ youth; some commentators say the young are more likely to follow prophets while elders cling to false religion.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r10.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r10.claim: God fortified their hearts by strengthening their patience and faith.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r11.speaker: Qu
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r11.claim: Another account adds that God strengthened their certitude.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r12.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r12.claim: Their rising refers to openly defying Daqyānūs and refusing his demand that they worship false deities.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r13.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r13.claim: They declared their Lord rules heaven and earth, while the tyrant’s false deities are merely subjects of the one Lord.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r14.speaker: IK, R
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r14.claim: In another account, the youths privately held belief in one God; their eldest confessed it when they met by chance outside the city.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r15.speaker: R, IK
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r15.claim: Finding the others agreed, they proclaimed their faith either immediately or after returning to the king’s court.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r2.claim: Younger Quraysh members were more likely than their elders to follow the Prophet.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r3.claim: Abraham’s youthful faith contrasts with his father’s idolatry; elsewhere community notables reject prophets.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r4.speaker: Q, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r4.claim: The word fatiyyah for youths is related to futuwwah, spiritual chivalry grounded in faith.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r5.speaker: Q, Su
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r5.claim: Futuwwah includes virtue, generosity, avoiding forbidden acts and harm, patience, truthfulness, freedom from hypocrisy, and detachment from worldly ties.

STUDYQURAN:18:13/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:13/r6.claim: The term futuwwah later became associated with guilds that cultivated these virtues.
